titleEn: You have rejected us; restore us
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Fourteen verses in the Hebrew numbering, the first two of them a heading that names a campaign. This is a communal lament after a military defeat, and it opens by saying out loud that God is the one who broke the line. In the middle an old oracle is quoted in which God parcels out the land like a man dividing a field, and the neighbouring kingdoms are reduced to a washbasin and a place to throw a sandal. Verses 7 to 14 appear again, almost unchanged, as Psalm 108:7 to 14. Watch the verb of verse 3: it comes back in verse 12 as a question.

stichs.en: For the leader; on shushan eduth.
A michtam of David, to teach.

verses.summary: The heading names a tune, a genre and a purpose. The last word says this was meant to be taught, which is why a defeat got written down at all.

stichs.en: When he fought Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah,
and Joab came back and struck Edom
in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand of them.

verses.summary: The heading dates the psalm to a war in the north and a battle in the south. The count given here differs from the parallel accounts in Samuel and Chronicles.

stichs.en: O God, You have rejected us, You have broken us open, You were angry.
Restore us.

verses.summary: Four verbs, three of them accusations and the fourth an imperative. The complaint is not that the enemy was strong but that God withdrew.

stichs.en: You made the land shake, You split it open.
Heal its fractures, for it is tottering.

verses.summary: The image shifts from an army to the ground itself. A land with fractures is a land after an earthquake, and the request is repair, not revenge.

stichs.en: You have shown Your people a hard thing;
You have made us drink wine that makes us reel.

verses.summary: Defeat is served as a drink. The verb is causative twice over: God is the one who showed and the one who poured.

stichs.en: You have given those who fear You a banner to raise,
because of the truth. Selah.

verses.summary: The one positive line in the first movement, and the hardest to translate. A banner is what a scattered army rallies to, so even here the picture is of troops that have broken.

stichs.en: So that Your beloved ones may be rescued,
save with Your right hand and answer me.

verses.summary: The plea proper, and the only place the speaker says me instead of us. The right hand is the fighting hand.

stichs.en: God has spoken in His holiness: let me exult.
I will parcel out Shechem and measure off the valley of Succoth.

verses.summary: God finally speaks, and the tone changes completely. The land is spoken of as property to be surveyed and divided, not territory to be fought over.

stichs.en: Gilead is mine and Manasseh is mine,
Ephraim is the stronghold of my head,
Judah is my commander's staff.

verses.summary: A roll call of the tribal holdings, north and south, each claimed with a possessive. Ephraim is armour, Judah is authority.

stichs.en: Moab is my washbasin,
on Edom I fling my sandal;
over me, Philistia, raise your shout.

verses.summary: The three neighbours get household treatment: a basin for washing, a spot to toss a sandal, a place to shout at. The oracle ends by making the enemies furniture.

stichs.en: Who will bring me to the fortified city?
Who has led me as far as Edom?

verses.summary: Back to the present, and back to doubt. The fortified city is unnamed, and the question is who is going to take the speaker there.

stichs.en: Is it not You, O God, who have rejected us?
And You do not go out, O God, with our armies.

verses.summary: The complaint of verse 3 returns as a question. Armies march out with their god at the head, and this one has not been marching out.

stichs.en: Give us help against the foe,
for the rescue that man gives is worthless.

verses.summary: The request is narrowed to one word: help. What comes after it is a judgment on every other source of help.

stichs.en: Through God we will do valiantly,
and He is the one who will trample our foes.

verses.summary: The last line does not say the defeat is reversed. It says who does the treading, and it is not the army.

pardes.body: Two verses of heading, then three movements. Verses 3 to 7 are the complaint and the plea, spoken to God. Verses 8 to 10 are a quotation, and the only place in the psalm where anyone but the speaker talks. Verses 11 to 14 return to the present and answer the oracle with a question. The hinge is {{8.1}}, the word for spoke: everything before it is addressed upward, and the confidence of the middle section belongs to a voice the speaker is repeating rather than one he currently hears. The last two verses accept the situation without claiming it has changed.

Three cruxes in nine verses. {{6.5}} is the Aramaic word for truth to most readers, which gives a banner raised because of the truth; others connect the consonants to the word for a bow and read a banner raised to flee the archers, and the ancient versions do not agree. {{9.8}} is built on the root for engraving and decreeing, so it is read as either a ruler's staff or a lawgiver, and both are current. {{10.9}} is a feminine imperative addressed to Philistia, a command to raise a shout, but the parallel line in Psalm 108 has a first person form, so the shout is either Philistia's submission or the speaker's triumph over her. The heading is a fourth crux: it credits Joab with twelve thousand in the valley named at {{2.12}}, while 2 Samuel 8 and 1 Chronicles 18 give eighteen thousand and Chronicles credits Abishai.

The oracle of verses 8 to 10 was read long after there was any land to divide, and read that way it stops being a war report and becomes a title deed: the tribal names are held in the present tense while the territory is gone, and the psalm's argument becomes the gap between the deed and the possession. The reuse of verses 7 to 14 inside Psalm 108, where they follow praise rather than complaint, is an early instance of that rereading. Verse 13 ends on {{13.6}}, and the whole point of the sentence is that this is the wrong noun to hope in. Verse 1 says the psalm exists to teach, and that is the lesson it teaches.

Read as a map of the divine attributes, the psalm moves from the side of severity to the side of kindness without pretending the severity was a mistake: God shakes the land in verse 4 and hands out a banner in verse 6, and both are the same hand. {{7.4}} names the right hand, which in kabbalistic idiom is the side of expansion and love, and the plea is that the fighting be done from there. The banner of verse 6 is the standing image for a sign lifted high enough to be seen from a distance, a gathering point for what has been scattered, which is what the whole psalm is asking for.
